phonemes.desc: Slender (palatalized) bilabial nasal [mʲ], the m pronounced with the tongue arched toward the hard palate — Old Irish distinguished slender from broad consonants throughout.
Long close front vowel [iː], the long í that modern editors mark with a síneadh fada when they print Mídir.
Lenited dental [ð], the soft voiced 'th' of English 'this'; Old Irish orthography writes the lenited consonant with a plain d.
Short unstressed [ɪ] closing in a slender (palatalized) tap [ɾʲ], the light final r of the o-stem name.

pronunciation.approximation: 'MEE-thir' — a long 'ee', the soft 'th' of 'this' for the d, and a whispered palatal r at the end. The modern Irish Mídír keeps essentially this sound.

pronunciation.note: Midir is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the temple form is plain ASCII, with no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to rescue. The fada in Mídir belongs to modern editorial convention, not to the manuscript norm that the project follows, and the mechanical rule judges the restored form, not the editorial one. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the god's standing in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: Underworld, Fairy King
domains.subtitle: The proud lord of the síd of Brí Léith
domains.lead: Midir — Old Irish Mídir, styled the Proud — is the lord of the síd of Brí Léith, the Otherworld mound by Ardagh in Longford, and the central figure of Tochmarc Étaíne, the Wooing of Étaín. His dossier is the strangest kind of kingship in the Irish corpus: not the spear or the plunder, but the board game, the wager, and the patience that spans a thousand and twelve years and two births of the same woman. He fostered [[aengus|Óengus]], the son of the young; he won Étaín Echraide by her father's impossible labors; he lost her to jealousy, found her again in another lifetime, and took her from the high king of Ireland at a game of fidchell played in the middle of Tara. Where other gods take what they want, Midir stakes, loses, waits, and wins.

cards.name: The Fidchell Board
cards.desc: The game of kings at which Midir sat across from Eochaid Airem in Tara, losing stake after stake until the board was set for the one prize he had come for.

cards.name: The Two Swans
cards.desc: The payment taken in flight: Midir and Étaín rising through Tara's smoke-hole as two swans linked by a silver chain, while the king's guard watched from the walls.

cards.name: Brí Léith
cards.desc: His síd by Ardagh in Longford — the mound Eochaid's host dug open in the war of the spades, and the hill the Dindsenchas names as his.

cards.name: The Scarlet Quicken-Rod
cards.desc: Fuamnach's jealous stroke in his own hall, which made Étaín a pool of water, a worm, and a purple fly — the malice his kingship could not keep out.

symbols.name: The fidchell board
symbols.meaning: The game of kings played at Tara — patience staked as strategy, and a wager that was really a judgment

symbols.name: The silver chain
symbols.meaning: The link between the two swans that rose through the smoke-hole of Tara — the bond the high king's host could not break

symbols.name: The sloe-thorn
symbols.meaning: The flying thorn that put out his eye at the Brug and set the whole wooing in motion — Dían Cécht healed the wound

symbols.name: Brí Léith
symbols.meaning: His síd by Ardagh in Longford, the mound the tales make his and the host of Ireland dug open to take Étaín back

symbols.name: The fifty women in one likeness
symbols.meaning: The riddle of resemblance at the mound's surrender — the deadliest answer the Otherworld ever gave a spade

mythology.lead: Midir's mythology is a single long courtship told in two lifetimes — the fullest Otherworld dossier in the Irish corpus, preserved entire in Tochmarc Étaíne. It begins with a sloe-thorn and a bride-price, passes through jealousy and transformation and a rebirth eleven hundred years later, and ends at a fidchell board in Tara and a war of spades against the hollow hills. Around that spine the tradition adds the fosterage: the lord of Brí Léith reared [[aengus|Óengus]], the Dagda's son, and the tie between the two mounds frames both gods' tales.

myths.title: The Sloe and the Bride-Price
myths.text:
Midir of Brí Léith was the foster-father of Óengus, and he came to Brú na Bóinne to visit his fosterling. While the boys of the Brug were at their hurling, a sloe-thorn sprang from the play and put out Midir's eye; he stayed a year in the mound while Dían Cécht, the physician of the Túatha Dé Danann, made him whole. For his reward and his heart's desire he named Étaín Echraide, daughter of Ailill, the fairest woman in Ireland — and it was Óengus who went to win her.

Her father Ailill mac Máta, king of the Ulaid, set a bride-price no mortal could pay: twelve plains cleared of their stones and wood, and twelve rivers led out of the land to the sea. Óengus performed the labors with the Dagda's strength behind him, and Midir brought Étaín home to Brí Léith as his wife. The tale's arithmetic is exact: the god's first possession of Étaín was bought by service, the price of a wounded eye — and it was the one part of the story that ended peaceably.

myths.title: The Fly in the Crystal Bower
myths.text:
Midir already had a wife: Fuamnach, foster-daughter of Bresal the druid, and versed in her foster-father's arts. When Étaín came home to Brí Léith, Fuamnach's jealousy found its instrument — a rod of scarlet quicken-tree — and one stroke made her rival a pool of water, then a worm, then a purple fly of wondrous size and sweetness. For seven years the fly that was Étaín went with Midir wherever he went, and he knew her in her shape; but Fuamnach's malice outlasted his keeping.

The fly came at last to Brú na Bóinne, where Óengus knew her and built her a grianán, a crystal sun-bower filled with healing herbs — until Fuamnach raised a magic wind that swept her across Ireland for seven years more, to fall into the cup of the wife of Étar, an Ulster warrior, at the Bay of Cíú. She was drunk, conceived, and born again a thousand and twelve years after her first birth: Étaín, daughter of Étar. Midir's house is the still center of the storm — the husband whose hall became the battlefield of two women's powers, and who waited out the centuries the tale demanded of him.

myths.title: The Long Game at Tara
myths.text:
In her second life Étaín married Eochaid Airem, high king of Ireland at Tara, and Midir came for her as the tale had promised. First he came in the shape of Ailill Anglonnach, the king's brother, who was wasting with love of her — three nights he lay beside her in that likeness and did not touch her, and so saved both her honor and Ailill's life. Then he revealed himself and asked her to come away with him; she answered that she would not go without her husband's leave. So Midir took the leave the hard way.

He came to Tara and challenged Eochaid to fidchell. Game after game Midir lost, and paid the stakes without stint — horses and treasures in such plenty that the king's greed was schooled by the god's purse. Then the board was set once more, and the stake named was an embrace and a kiss from Étaín; Midir won. Eochaid deferred the payment for a month, and when the month was out Tara stood ringed with warriors and the house barred. Midir appeared all the same in the midst of the hall, sang to Étaín the invitation to the wondrous land, took her in his arms, and the two rose through the smoke-hole as two swans linked by a silver chain, while the host of Ireland watched from the ramparts and could do nothing.

myths.title: The Fifty Women in One Likeness
myths.text:
Eochaid's answer was the spade: he set the men of Ireland to digging up the síd-mounds one by one, a war of delving against the hollow hills, until the host stood over Brí Léith itself. Then Midir came to the parley, and the bargain struck was surrender of a kind: on the morrow fifty women came out of the mound, every one of them in Étaín's exact likeness, and the king was told to choose his wife.

He chose — and chose his own daughter, born to Étaín in the síd and hidden in the likeness of her mother. By that unwitting union a daughter was conceived who was exposed and spared, reared as Mess Búachalla, the cowherd's fosterling, and through her the line ran down to Conaire Mór, the doomed king of the Bruiden Da Derga. When Midir revealed the deception he gave back the true Étaín as well; the tale lets the god keep the last word and the king keep his shame. It is the Otherworld's coldest jest: the wager was never about the game, and the digging was never going to win.

myths.title: The Foster-Father of the Young God
myths.text:
Behind the wooing stands the fosterage. When the Dagda divided the síd-mounds of Ireland among the Túatha Dé Danann, his son Óengus was away with Midir of Brí Léith, being fostered, and received nothing — the absence that led to the famous quibble of the day and the night, and to Brú na Bóinne passing to the son. The tradition thus ties the two mounds together from the beginning: the young god reared at Brí Léith, the proud god's eye healed at the Brug.

The foster-bond runs both ways through the dossier. It was for Midir that Óengus won Étaín Echraide and performed her father's labors; it was in Óengus's bower that Étaín the purple fly found her one refuge. Irish fosterage was no light tie — it stood beside blood, and the tales honor it. Midir's proudest title is not lord of Brí Léith but the one the stories keep proving: the man who raised the son of the young.

lore.syncretism: Midir has no cross-border witness of his own, and the honest comparison is typological rather than genetic. No Gaulish altar names him and no scholar has proposed one; where the Dagda can be set beside Sucellos on the strength of club and cauldron, Midir's dossier — the wager, the hunted bride, the mound that is a court — belongs to the Otherworld-king figure-type that Mac Cana and Sjoestedt trace through the Celtic materials without anchoring it to any single epigraphic god. Within Ireland his structural kin are the síd-lords of the neighboring tales: Bodb Derg of the Munster síde, who answers the Dagda's search in the Aislinge, and [[manannan|Manannán]], the sea-going master of the Otherworld's glamour. The Welsh corpus offers only a functional parallel — [[arawn|Arawn]], the lord of Annwn who likewise binds a mortal king by a bargain with a hidden edge — and the parallel is a pattern, not a pedigree. The comparisons instruct; none of them identifies him.
lore.culturalLegacy: Midir's afterlife is the afterlife of Tochmarc Étaíne itself, the tale that never let him go. P. W. Joyce carried 'The Wooing of Etain' into modern English in Old Celtic Romances (1879), and Lady Gregory made the fidchell game and the swans part of the Celtic revival's furniture in Gods and Fighting Men (1904). James Stephens gave the story its strangest modern retelling in In the Land of Youth (1924), where Midir's arrival at Tara is staged as high comedy turning to awe. Bergin and Best's edition in Ériu (1938) fixed the text for scholarship, and Jeffrey Gantz's Penguin translation (1981) put the whole dossier on the general reader's shelf, where it has stayed: the fidchell game is now the standard citation whenever Irish literature wants to prove that its gods play a longer game than its kings. The name itself took no second path — no Angus, no Brigit: Midir never became a given name, a place, or a pub, and remains what the manuscripts made him, a proper noun with a single bearer.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Midir is the god of the long game, and the tradition tells you so in his name before it tells you in his story: the handbooks gloss it, cautiously, as judge — and a judge is exactly what a wager needs. Watch how he plays Eochaid. He loses, and loses, and pays without stint, because the losses are the lesson: the king is being taught that the man across the board can afford anything, that the stakes are a language, and that the only sentence being written is the last one. When the final stake is named — an embrace, a kiss — the game has already been won for a month. The fidchell board is a court, and the house always already holds the verdict.

That patience is the Otherworld's whole tempo. A mortal wooing is measured in seasons; Midir's spans a thousand and twelve years, two births of the same woman, and a war of spades against his own roof — and he never hurries, because time is the one currency his kind does not spend. His foster-son [[aengus|Óengus]] parses time into a loophole and holds a mound on a day without a term; the foster-father plays time into a stake and holds a woman across two lifetimes. Between them the síd of Ireland teaches the same doctrine: the hollow hills do not take what they want. They wait until the wanting itself concedes.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in medieval Irish manuscripts in the Insular Latin script as Midir — the spelling Bergin and Best print from Lebor na hUidre; many modern editors add the fada and write Mídir to mark the long vowel, an editorial convention rather than the manuscript norm. The earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the restored form is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: midir.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Midir is a textual god — no ogham stone names him and no votive inscription invokes him — but both halves of his mythic geography are real and visitable. Brí Léith is a hill by Ardagh in County Longford, the mound the Dindsenchas names as his síd, and the surrounding Longford bogland preserves one of the showpiece monuments of the Irish Iron Age: the Corlea Trackway, a massive oak togher across the bog a few miles south of Ardagh, excavated under Barry Raftery and fixed by dendrochronology to 148–147 BCE — a road of the very centuries in which the síd-lord's landscape was being imagined. The tale's other stage is Tara in County Meath, where the earthworks of Ráith na Rí, the Forrad, and the long banquet-hall trench called Tech Midchúarta still ridge the hill on which Eochaid Airem kept his court and lost his wager. The manuscript witnesses are exact: Tochmarc Étaíne is preserved, incompletely, in the twelfth-century Lebor na hUidre (RIA MS 23 E 25) and completed in the fifteenth-century Yellow Book of Lecan, the twin bases of Bergin and Best's edition; the companion Aislinge Óenguso survives in the fifteenth-century British Library MS Egerton 1782, the basis of Shaw's.
